utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you are to continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, before we return to a broadly chronological line of questioning, one overall sweep on a particular topic, and it's this: In the society of which you were a policeman, assassination was common, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I'm not receiving the interpretation. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the society of which you were a policeman, assassination was common, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I mean in this sense, to be specific: That over the years between 1997 and 2000, in particular, assassination of significant people was a not uncommon event.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Serbia, there were, of course, killings, that is true. However, the greatest frequency of killings was perpetrated by the terrorists in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to focus on that first section, the ones in Serbia, because there were several of them, and they either go undetected altogether or they're attribute to the MUP. Shall I list some? There was your boss Badza, who was assassinated in 1997. Moving on to 1999, there was the famous journalist Slavko Curuvija gunned down in his wife's company. Then there were the most famous liberal lawyers, Kelmendi and Agani. Then coming to 2000, you have Pavle Bulatovic, a former minister. You have Arkan, and indeed Stambolic and Djindjic. These are just some of the assassinations that characterised your society, and they've either gone apparently unresolved or they've been levelled at, in three cases, people from the MUP. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those killings that you mentioned I do, of course, know about. Investigations in all these cases of killing was conducted as soon as the killings took place. Up until the present time, I'm not certain whether any of those killings have been solved, those cases solved, but I do know that the police is working on all those cases and some of them are being processed in court as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prosecuted, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You sought to match your police force with, for example, the police force of a country like France. Can you point to any Northern European or Western society which has the level and incidence of unsolved assassinations of top people of the kind I've just briefly reviewed?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there are unsolved assassinations in Western countries too. For Serbia, the important thing is that Serbia, during this period of time, was confronted with extreme security related problems and risks which affected, in other things, this increase in the number of murders, in additional ones -- including the ones you mentioned. But Serbia was facing very specific circumstances during that period. They were circumstances not caused by Serbia. The war affected the situation in Serbia to make it deteriorate and that the police had to focus on preventing the war from moving into --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your answer may be a partial answer but let me just ask you this blunt question: Is any of the assassinations I've identified associated with the KLA or are they all associated in the public mind and public discussion with people in Serbia, frequently with the MUP?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every assassination, until it is solved, or any killing and murder until it is solved can give rise to a series of different versions as to what happened. Versions and assumptions in the police force are a component part of policework. Now, the result of police investigation and court investigations or investigations in general is to uncover the perpetrator, just as it is to punish the perpetrator and that is the business of the courts. Until the investigations are completed --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... associated in the public mind with the KLA. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In public, in the public mind, as far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I return, as we look at things chronologically, to the proposition that this was indeed a police state and a police state becoming ever more extreme as the 1990s passed, and I explore this topic in the course of my questioning for this reason which I'd like your help with --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you accept from your knowledge of the world generally and from the knowledge of the state in which you operated that where the police or any other otherwise authorised user of force acts with impunity two things follow: The population lives in fear. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Serbia, the police did not act with impunity. Fear in Serbia was caused primarily by terrorism. Fear was the ultimate goal of terrorism on the medium level. Of course, tactically speaking, the object of terrorism was violence and killing. The source of fear in Serbia was dominantly based in terrorism and the fear that the war would spread to the territory of Serbia. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well, I have your answer.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- working of the police was the consequence and reaction of that kind of situation and the way in which fear was stoked, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You realise, and you're going to realise as we look at one or two bits of film, I'm not uniquely concerned with fear in Kosovo, I'm also interested in fear in Belgrade. Now, you're not suggesting, are you, that people in Belgrade were living in fear of KLA terrorism, are you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People in Belgrade, too, lived with the fear that the war would spread to Serbia. They lived in fear of what would happen in Kosovo. They lived in fear of what the terrorists in Kosovo were doing that might be -- might spread to Belgrade, and they would start doing that there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second consequence of the two I said I would ask you about of a police state, as you know, is that a political leader with a police force that can act with impunity need only tilt his head or give a general direction and he will know that his wishes will be carried out, even unlawfully, by such a police force. Now, that's a general proposition. Do you accept it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise, but once again you have two or three assertions that you're making which make it difficult for me to follow, but let me repeat that we cannot speak about a police state in any event. And secondly, let me say that the police, to the best of my knowledge and information - as you know I was assistant minister - the police never listened to what politicians said and looked at the tilts of their heads. The minister would create the policy of the ministry together with his advisors. And as a member of the ministry myself, I followed orders and guidelines from the minister. Now, the third part of your question, as to whether they were unlawfully carried out, his wishes unlawfully carried out, I can say that I just received lawful orders, not unlawful orders, and I did not execute therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you wouldn't mind --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- any unlawful orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... focussed on and related to my questions. Now, let me make clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that question wasn't amenable to a short answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think one has to be fair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look again at tab 6. We had looked at it before. We have never had a translation coming from the Defence side. I have a rough translation, which I'm afraid I've marked, but if it can just go on the overhead projector, and if the witness can take tab 6, please. So that we understand the structure in which you operated as between the public security and secret service - it has no translation - we discussed this briefly the other day, Article 20 is along the following lines -- first of all, Article 17 requires: Employees - that's employees of the MUP - who do not know each other to introduce themselves. Article 20 says that the employee - this is a MUP employee - has the responsibility to warn another employee of his sector who is acting contrary to this Code of Conduct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let the witness have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He has it in front of him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Tab 6. And I'm looking at Article 20.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have Article 20 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Article 20 is along the lines that: "The employee has the responsibility to warn another employee of his sector who is acting contrary to this Code of Conduct, but also to inform his supervisor. When an employee from another sector is in contradiction with the code, the supervisor will inform the organ with whom the employee is associated." Now, this is a formal way, is it not, of requiring different parts of the DB to require each other to behave legally?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thus, if you as a member of the public security at any time became aware of illegal acts by the DB, it would be your duty to report it.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Particularly as you were a senior police officer. There's no way you could excuse or turn a blind eye to illegality in the secret police.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I wasn't able to turn a blind eye towards illegality on the part of anybody, but I claim that I never did turn a blind eye faced with any illegality on the part of anyone, not only members of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I can have that back, please, Mr. Prendergast.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In 1992, various things coincided. Let me remind you of what General Vasiljevic told us in part when he was here giving evidence. He said that in April of 1992, Stanisic so organised events as for there to be a single security service; namely, the security service of Serbia. That was done in part by appointing a man called Nedeljko Boskovic to the state security -- to the military security service. Do you remember those events?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any event surrounding the man Nedeljkovic, if I remember the name correctly -- or Boskovic. I do not remember anything about that man related to 1992. If you jog my memory, perhaps that will help me remember something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Stanisic told us that his being appointed to the position that he was given was a way of making military security intelligence available effectively to this accused, and he linked it with the takeover of the MUP building, the federal MUP building, in Serbia by the Serb MUP. Let's go and deal with that in the two stages. Do you know anything about the changes in the military security service brought about by the change in positions of Nedeljko Boskovic?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of all the things that you have just stated in these several sentences, all I know is what relates to taking over security in the federal MUP building during 1992. I know none of any of the other things that you have set forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Boskovic to remind the Court, succeeded Vasiljevic in May of 1992, and we will now indeed turn to the takeover of the MUP building. What was the purpose of that takeover?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of the takeover of security of the MUP building was that the organisational units and resources of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, which were located in that building, in that facility, should be secured in the proper way, provided security. And before that, the leadership of the federal Ministry of the Interior was opposed to a certain extent to that before. But let me repeat: That was the building and facility in which certain units of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia were located as well as sensitive equipment used by the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The territorial or security justification was all a sham, wasn't it? This was a way that this accused could get control of federal MUP archives and intelligence. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely not true. According to all the information that I have, and I took part directly in that operation, I know full well Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. what units were located there. Well, I don't know exactly their names, but I know who their leaders were, I know which equipment was there, and I also know that there was a contract between the federal and republican Ministry of the Interior which implied and meant that the republican MUP in that space used the largest amount of the premises there apart from what was already in existence there before. And apart from security itself, the object was to enter the premises provided for on the basis of that contract and agreement and which was to be used by the republican Secretariat for the Interior or, rather, the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, now --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it was -- what you said a moment ago is absolutely incorrect. At no point in time did I have any information that in relation to -- that the president of the Republic of Serbia had information in that regard and related to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware of the existence of something called the Council for Reconciliation on Standpoints Regarding State Politics, sometimes called by a slightly different name, but were you aware of that, the existence and the functioning of that council?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's a body for which we have been provided with some stenographic records. Before I come to the stenographic record concerned, because it may be that I have failed to alert Ms. Dicklich to the possibility of wanting to look at this one, and to deal with a general point, do you know where records of important bodies such as the Council for Harmonisation or the Supreme Defence Council, do you know where those records are kept?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have to know whose council you are referring to. I'm not able to identify it by the name you have given. Is it a federal authority? Is it a municipal authority? Is it a governmental body? Whose organ is it? That's what I need to know in order to be able to reply. If there is a different name, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Generally, is it right that for important government bodies there's a statutory requirement to keep records and to keep them in more than one place in order that they may be preserved for posterity? Is there a general requirement that that should happen?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which regulations governed that. I know about the Ministry of the Interior, that there are regulations governing the archiving and safekeeping of documentation. How it works in other bodies, in other authorities, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, we've been provided only with the minutes of a particular meeting, the meeting that covers the takeover of the MUP building, not with the stenographic records themselves, and I was going to see if you could help us know how that could have been and whether any such important document could have been destroyed or not, but you don't seem able to help. I'll have to read you a short passage from the minute that we have been provided with. It's tab 45, I think. 469 is the Exhibit number. And to assist you, this was a body presided over by Dobrica Cosic, attended by this accused, President Bulatovic, Milan Panic, and various others, and it said this, this is about six lines that I must read out: "On the 18th of October of this year, 1992, officers of the republic Ministry of Internal Affairs forcefully occupied the building of the federal ministry. Once inside, they prohibited employees of the state security service of the federal Ministry of Internal Affairs to enter their offices." And then this: "Taking over the building, the officers also took over its communications system, its system of crypt-protection, all equipment and technical devices of the state security service." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would have to ask you again not to ask me several questions in the framework of one question. Otherwise, I will have to make notes before I answer. However, in this case, most of these statements are not true. First of all, there was no occupation of the building, one. Second, none of the employees in the federal Ministry of the Interior were prevented from reaching their workplaces. What happened was that a new reception desk and a new system of checking IDs and official cards was set up. The purpose of the action was to take over the security provided in the building, the equipment, and the archives. This security means also the regime of entry and exit from the building. That system was changed within one day. And the next day the employees did not accept that system, and that's the reason why they didn't go into their offices, some of them. The majority accepted the system and went to work in their offices. I don't know what else was included in your question, but I remembered these two details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Earlier you spoke of a contract that was a part of the takeover. I didn't understand what that was all about. Could you explain that for me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will explain, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I receive that document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose the witness should also have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let a copy of the document be passed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It's an existing exhibit in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll bring it down at the break and make sure it's available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you'll receive a copy soon. Would you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the witness should also receive a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If the witness wants to have a copy to facilitate his answer, yes, he should have it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I am going to continue to answer questions related to that document, of course I should like to have a copy, but let me continue. For a while, perhaps for several months before this takeover of security in the building of the federal Secretariat for Internal Affairs, the federal secretary, or minister - I don't know how the position was called at the time - and the republican minister of the interior had signed a contract. The subject of that contract was a lease of the greatest part of offices in the federal building to the republican ministry. Part of their office space and part of the equipment of the federal Ministry of the Interior at the moment of takeover was already in possession of certain units within the republican Ministry of the Interior of Serbia. Pending was the takeover of the remaining office space, subject to the contract. However, in the council of ministers, in the agreement between ministers, certain problems had occurred and these problems had not been entirely solved at the time when the takeover took place. I don't know if this was a clear enough answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the takeover was in fulfilment of the terms of a contract.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You could say that. And the fulfilment of those terms of contract had already taken place at the time of takeover. In other words, the contract was partially executed at the moment of takeover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... may not be the right word then. It has a certain connotation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said takeover of security, of the building, equipment and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They assumed certain --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- contract.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In keeping with the contract. We have a different term for takeover. We say "seizure" if we mean something else. There was no violence. That's one more thing that I want to mention. Mr. Prosecutor mentioned violence. Not in one single case was there any violence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were in charge of this operation, and indeed you --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- you accepted at one stage that, even if not violently, there had been disarming by your troops of the federal staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in part. Out of an abundance of caution, to prevent any type of violence, armed members of the federal MUP were asked to hand over their ammunition, to be precise. They kept their weapons. And not in a single case was that done violently, because when one uses the term "disarm," one usually means violent disarming.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... unlawful takeover and I'm going to ask you some questions now about what Dobrica Cosic has written about this. Do you have any reason to doubt what Dobrica Cosic might recall about these events, before we look at what he said?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hold Mr. Cosic in high esteem, but in order to be able to speak about his positions, I would have to know them first, and I would have to know the source of his positions. Maybe he was misinformed or labouring under misconceptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the absence of a sufficiency of photocopies - my responsibility entirely - may the witness have a photocopy of the Cyrillic version and may the matching English-language versions go on the overhead projector. This is from his latest book. We can just read a few passages, starting, please, at 193. You see page 193 in the book. Mr. Cosic records this: "We sat at the council meeting for nine hours, arguing about the take-over of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Ministry of State Security, which was under the orders of Slobodan Milosevic. In addition to this take-over, pressure was exerted on the workers of SDB Yugoslavia in order to convince them to come to work for the Ministry of State Security." And then this: "Milosevic is taking control over all mechanisms of state authority." Next page, please, Mr. Prendergast. Page 177, he records it in these terms: "I came back from Geneva before midnight. While I was away on the trip, Milosevic forcefully took control over the Ministry of State Security." Next page, please, Mr. Prendergast. 178, Mr. Stevanovic: "That is an upheaval ... Matovic informed me how the deed was done. That is an event which I cannot accept without adequate resistance." Next page, please, Mr. Prendergast, I think the last. "I did not go to the office today. I did not have the strength to listen to people. In these last three days there were too many events which occurred for me to be able to write them in my notebook. I am shocked at Milosevic's act which he committed while I was away in Geneva. His police forcefully entered the building of Ministry of Internal Affairs and into the rooms belonging to the Ministry of State Security. They disarmed the police, took over the command technology, documents, archives, and they threw out the workers. The country was left without a Ministry of State Security, which deprived the state of one of the main Constitutional functions. The tyrant from Pozarevac committed this uprising ... when Panic and I were out of the country. What is that man thinking? The destructive coup against this sovereign state was committed under the command of the chief of the SDB Serbia and with the knowledge of the executive person for General Staff and Kos. The event received much publicity. The event decreased the authority within the country and internationally of Panic and myself." Now, that's the way the president, who was taken unaware as being out of the country, viewed this, and you were the officer in charge. You were assisting this accused as early as the late autumn of 1992 in his attempt to take over all organs of power. That's my question to you.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that, too, is a very complicated question, but let me say first that all this that you have read is something I'm hearing for the first time, and with all due respect the only thing I can say is that this is a political qualification of an event that is based, in my opinion, on facts that are simply wrong. I never thought that such commentary was possible on that incident. Maybe the whole thing was too politicised to make this comment, this type of comment possible. But some of the facts are maybe correct. I would, however, appreciate a more precise question. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which ones do you say may be correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the fact that we took over the security in the building is correct, but that this amounted to a coup is not correct. That this act prevented the employees of the federal ministry from continuing to work is not correct. That action amounted to taking over premises that were in the possession of the republican ministry. Premises belonging to the federal ministry were not taken nor were their powers taken away from them. It was a simple -- no, it wasn't a simple, it was a complex police intervention. But on the same grounds and in the same way, the police lends assistance to other bodies and authorities in the execution of their obligations. In this case, there was a decision of the state security sector to take over security. The public security sector only acted in compliance with Article 10 of the law on state powers as an executive body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, at page 183, there's a reference to the coup being committed under the command of the chief of SDB Serbia. Does the witness know who that was, the chief of SDB Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 it was Mr. Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And -- and since you were the officer in charge of the takeover, is it right, as the article by Mr. Cosic suggests, that you were acting on his instructions?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose instructions, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Stanisic's.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whose instructions were you acting on, then?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I acted upon the instructions of the then deputy minister, Mr. Stojicic, because he was my superior yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not clear to me, Mr. Nice, whether one is to understand that passage as meaning that Mr. Stanisic was actually present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, I don't think that is intended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not the intention. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I clarify something? I'm not understanding some of this at all. The contract that you referred to, would that have left part of the building under the control of the federal Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As a result of what happened on this occasion, did they remain in control of any part of the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they did. They kept supervision over the part of the building that they were using. The federal MUP continued, even after that operation, to use that building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That means that, according to you, what is said by Cosic, that the country was left without the Ministry of State Security, which deprived the state of one of the main constitutional functions, is wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether that is wrong or not. I know it's not accurate. The federal ministry continued to exist. This action --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Within that building. That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Part of the building remained available to the federal ministry, and the federal ministry continued to be. So this action in no way made the federal ministry disappear in itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would that contract be available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am certain that a copy exists, unless it was destroyed during the bombing. Unfortunately, the building and the archives of the MUP of Serbia were both destroyed, just as the building of the federal ministry, but I believe that the contract can be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I have the documents back, please, Mr. Prendergast.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move on, I just want to move back in time to something I meant to show you a little earlier. It's a short clip from a television production called The Death of Yugoslavia, if we can just play it, and it relates to a date in March 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] -- was surprised because the demonstration he saw on television, though massive, was peaceful. He refused to vote for bringing in the army. Soon after this, the Serb police were sent in." "[Serbian spoken] "The Serb leaders at first asked for tanks to be put on the streets three hours earlier. Now their case was stronger."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What we saw of the behaviour of the police as early as 1991 typical of the behaviour of your police when dealing with demonstrators, was it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was typical for the police of Serbia was to take certain measures in case of violent demonstrations. Such demonstrations occurred both in Belgrade and in Pristina, sometimes at the same time. But I still don't understand the point of your question. Every police force acts in a similar way faced with such demonstrations, depending only on the intensity of violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is your understanding that that sort of response is what you'd find in Norway, England, Germany, to take three countries at random?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak about particular states, but I believe that in most states the response of the police to violent demonstrations is similar. Violent steps are possible, and in Serbia there was a tendency to generalise them. One single sequence is sometimes multiplied ten times on television to create an impression about the actions of a police force. Such impressions are incorrect. There are many instances of footage where you can see the police force facing demonstrators for three months without taking a single violent step.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... that question, because I've seen responses like that in Western countries. It all depends on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whether they were generated, as was asserted there, or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But another respective event that I want to remind the Chamber of through you and see if you have any comments on it, very briefly, is this: Do you remember that towards the end of 1991, as we've heard from a witness in this court, Gajic-Glisic, there was an attempt to create a Ministry of Defence of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you are referring to, but I know that there existed a Ministry of Defence of Serbia in a certain period. I am, however, unable to specify which period that was. But about any attempts to create one, that's something I really can't tell you anything about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, the Ministry of Defence of Serbia didn't last for long and came to very little, and by the end of 1992, which is roughly where we started this morning, my suggestion to you is that, with your assistance, the accused had the MUP at his control, had intelligence at his fingertips, and was moving to ever greater control of all organs of power. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to MUP, I do not accept that. I never had such an impression. But it is quite natural for the president of Serbia to have certain rights, such as to require reports from the minister of defence of Serbia or the minister of the interior. But I believe that the attitude of state authorities, including the president, towards the MUP was absolutely not unusual in Serbia compared to other countries. As to what the MUP was going to do, those kinds of decisions were made in the MUP itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The case against this accused includes that from this time onwards, approximately, not sure of the VJ, or the JNA or then the VJ, he relied upon and sought the enlargement of authority of the MUP. That's the case in part. And I want to read you what General Vasiljevic told us in a very short passage about what happened from the end of 1992. He said this, and I want you to hear it and then tell me if it's accurate or not: "... from 1993 onwards, the MUP of Serbia was considerably enlarged. First and foremost, in view of the various MUP units that were being formed and that practically constitute a small-scale army over which absolute authority was exercised by the accused through Stojicic and through the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia." Now, what do you say to those sentences of Vasiljevic, a former general?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement by General Vasiljevic absolutely does not correspond to the truth. I don't know in what way he is able to claim that the MUP was enlarged. For 20 years the MUP had the same number of men. It was of the same strength. It had special units as of 1972. The Ministry of the Interior had a special unit as of 1979. Therefore, nothing serious in organisational terms was changed, except for the fact that the MUP, after 1989, was centralised in organisational terms. Everything else can be considered as being the same organisation, the same complement of forces as it was before the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Vasiljevic went on, and this is on the 6th of February of 2003 when he was a witness, he went on to say: "It was practically combat units that were established, with helicopters, with weapons that are not characteristic of what the police usually has. Special purpose units were established and some officers of the Yugoslav army were taken over, especially from the military police, those who were specialists in particular operations and also helicopter pilots." He concluded: "An imposing armada was established consisting of tens of thousands of persons." I'll break it down for you. He says effectively combat units were established. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Of course not. Let me repeat: Those units of that kind of structure and of that kind of purpose, with that kind of equipment and uniforms had existed since 1972. Helicopters in the police force of Serbia existed before I entered the police force. When I came to the Ministry of the Interior, the police already had helicopters at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... taking over of some army officers?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in individual cases. For pilots, because it was logical that the Ministry of the Interior should, in some other way -- that it was difficult for them to find pilots. Otherwise, the police did train a number of pilots, but it take over a number of pilots from the army on the basis of a regular competition, opening posts for pilots in agreement with the General Staff. But that was a small number, five or six pilots at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, in 1993 -- and I remind you that you have compared your police force favourably with other Northern European police forces, and I want your help with the following: Human rights organisations were reporting on the former Yugoslavia right throughout the 1990s, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of some reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In particular, Mazowiecki was reporting to the United Nations, Human Rights Watch reports were being published, and the Humanitarian Law Fund in Belgrade was publishing reports. These documents were either made publicly available or were specifically sent to ministries and to the president of Serbia for action. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was sent to the president of Serbia I really can't say. I don't know. But I do know that the police of Serbia did have some of those documents, and I personally, if you find that important, had a discussion with Mr. Izbir [phoen], a conversation with him. I don't know what post he occupied at the time. And secondly, quite certainly every event which those organisations dealt with in their reports were the subject of attention and investigation by the police; they checked it out. And I said in response to one of your previous questions that the only problem was with very bias and one-sided and incorrect reporting of certain facts from the report from the Fund for Humanitarian Law which was based on superficial, incorrect, and insufficiently checked out data and information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just give me a minute, please. Can we just look, then, please - I'm afraid they're in English. They will be laid on the overhead projector. I shall identify when they're existing exhibits and I shall identify when they're not - at some of the reporting, for example, for 1993. The first one is a document that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is exhibited, and it is Exhibit 772. And if we can just put the index - thank you very much - on the overhead projector. And the contents, Mr. Prendergast. We can see the contents itself. Sorry, turn over to the next page, please. We see the heading -- okay. Don't bother with the contents. Move on to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you expect me to be able to follow, I should like to ask you for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we go back to what's numbered page 36 in the top left-hand corner, Mr. Prendergast, please, and that's all I need trouble us with at the moment. We needn't trouble with the index. Page 36 at the top left-hand corner. There are we. And "Police Brutality," if we could look at that passage there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm just going to read you something that came from a report, this report being published for the United Nations, and it says: "Several reports indicate that before and after the elections of 20 December 1992, the police adopted a more severe and aggressive attitude towards the Albanian population." And then in the first sentence of the next paragraph, paragraph 161, it says: "Police action has gone beyond arrest and imprisonment and cases of death as a result of shooting or brutality by the police have been reported." Well, now, that's a summary. Was this report investigated, Mr. Stevanovic, this report going to the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I not aware of this report, so I can't say whether it was or was not. If in any way it reached the Ministry of the Interior, then quite certainly it was. But what you've just read out is rather generalised and I claim that with respect to any elections in the Republic of Serbia the police never undertook additional, especially not violent, steps towards the Albanians, and I understand that's what it says in this particular text.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next document I want you to consider, which is our Exhibit 205.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I consider that Mr. Nice must provide a translation for the witness if he is going to base his questions on a specific document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, maybe the documents then should be placed on the -- on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These documents are available to us in English, although I suspect originally served on the Yugoslav authorities in -- probably -- no, I'm not sure about that document. That document may only ever have been in English, actually, served on the authorities. The next report, the Human Rights Watch report, similarly is in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I check at this moment. The previous one was 772?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it translated ever?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of that I'm not aware. It's a United Nations document. You mean was it translated in court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the purpose of disclosure, whether it was translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. As an exhibit, of course, it has to be in one of the languages of the Tribunal and they don't have to be translated, and I'm not sure that it would have been translated, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we can look at this next document. I'll just explain to you, Mr. Stevanovic, what it is. It's a Human Rights Watch report and published in New York but circulated, as we've heard from the author of this report or similar reports, to government offices. And if Mr. Prendergast would be good enough to take us, please, to top right-hand side corner page 15.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you give me the date of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can. The date of the report was March of 1993. I think that can't be right. It's 1993, and the reason I say that can't be right is because I'm looking at something on page 15 that relates to August with a footnote in October 1993. So the report itself must have a later date. But the allegation that is being made - and this is a sample, Mr. Stevanovic - on page 15 says: "On August 25, 1993, police shot and killed sixteen-year-old Sefer Qukovci in ..." a particular Albanian village, and then sets out the detail. Can you tell me, please, how in your 17 binders of materials I'm going to be able to track how -- whether and how such an allegation was ever investigated?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In these 17 binders you certainly won't find that, but you will certainly find that in the 1.015 files in the MUP. Of course, the number is not the right number, I just chose it to illustrate my point. On the one hand, you're criticising me for bringing in all this voluminous material and on the other hand you're asking for more material and more documents. I wasn't able to bring in the whole of the MUP archives with me, and I'm quite certain that if you wish to know exactly, then you should ask the MUP what was done specifically with respect to that case. At this point in time I really can't remember the event or tell you about it, but I can say with certainty --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He didn't finish his sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well, can say with certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Conclude the sentence now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I can say with certainty that if the document reached the MUP, and I do believe it did, then I'm quite sure that this case was investigated and that the results of that investigation exist. And I asked you intentionally the date of this document because, if you recall, I have been explaining over the past days that at the beginning of 1993 and the entire part of 1993 I spent in Bajina Basta, in that area of Rudo, Priboj, et cetera, so that I do believe that that period of time is something I recall -- actually, I recall less what was at MUP headquarters at the time because I dealt with the border problems and problems between the municipalities of Visegrad, Rudo, Visegrad and Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, is that report an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This report is an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This report is an exhibit. It's 205. Page 18, please, Mr. Prendergast.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, here we have a record of how policemen were dealt with on one occasion, and I'll summarise the history for you. It's the murder of Arif Krasniqi in the Prizren police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we're considering this matter of translation. The particular document which was exhibited in your case and, therefore, would have had to be disclosed to the accused, that was not translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. There's never been any requirement for translation into B/C/S of exhibits that come in in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That come in in English or French.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: French, yes. And indeed it would be a very, very, very large task to bring that about. Nor has it been the subject of complaint by the accused or the amicus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There was, in fact, an issue concerning the provision of trial documents to the accused in B/C/S. At the start of the proceedings in June of 2001, July of 2001, originally it was the intention of the Prosecution to only supply documents in the English language. The amicus objected to that in October 2001, and there was a ruling by the Trial Chamber that the materials for trial be provided in his language, B/C/S, so that he was more familiar with the contents, and that was the order of the Tribunal. I've been unaware that any documents such as the Human Rights Watch documents we're looking at at the moment, which came from Fred Abrahams, which were obviously written by that organisation in the language that it uses, the English language, that they had not been translated into B/C/S as part of the Court-provided documents for trial. It was the understanding that documents be provided for trial in the language of the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to what Mr. Nice said, that there were no objections regarding the documents from me, let me remind you and Mr. Kwon - at the time the Presiding Judge was another - that I on several occasions did object and complain because of the vast quantity of documents that I was being given, and my objections were that I was being given them untranslated. I assume that the results of that objection of mine was the Trial Chamber decision that I be provided with translated documents, so what Mr. Nice just said is not correct, that there were no objections. There were certainly objections, but of course they were ignored, despite the Trial Chamber's decision and ruling in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the matter to which Mr. Kay referred related to supporting materials, and I think that the practice in respect of exhibits since then has been as I outlined it. That's all I have to say on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will endeavour to find the order which was made and will carry out further investigations into this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Continue, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Stevanovic, in this report we have - it's at page 18 if Mr. Prendergast could follow us through - the account of the death of a man called Arif Krasniqi, where he was interrogated in Prizren police station, where his interrogation was witnessed, and where two police officers, one of whom was called Jasovic but with a different first name, Momir, another was Tihomir, and as a result of his beating in prison he died. Slavisa Dobricanin conducted the autopsy. Two officers were -- two officers were charged. And if Mr. Prendergast will take us to page 20, the summary of the trial is reflected in this way: "Fellow policemen warmly greeted Jasovic and Kosovic as they arrived in the courtroom for the trial on November 23, 1993, and threatened the Krasniqi family's lawyers. After a short trial, the court found Jasovic and Kosovic guilty and sentenced them both to three years imprisonment, but immediately released them pending their appeal." Now, does that sound a reasonable description? Well, first of all, do you know of this trial itself? You were a senior policeman at the time. Do you know of this trial?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of this trial, although I have the impression that I do seem to recall the event but possibly I have mixed it up with another event. I thought that this event related to Kosovska Mitrovica, in fact. But -- what was it you were wanting to ask me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My question to you was does this sound a reasonable description of how police officers would be dealt with for killing someone in the course of interrogating him: Three-year sentence, released immediately on appeal. Is that the way your society was operating?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With your permission, I don't wish to respond to your term "society." I don't know what you mean by "society." I know how the police functioned, and as far as the police is concerned, everything is quite clear here. The police, obviously, threw light on the event, established or, rather, concluded that there was reasonable doubt that these policemen had overstepped their authority which led to the death of an individual, and quite obviously they filed a criminal report, and quite obviously again, everything was given over to the court, and the court is independent in the Republic of Serbia vis-a-vis the executive powers and authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How can you kill someone by overstepping your authority? What could you be doing to someone at all that leads to his death merely because you slightly overdo it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Overstepping one's authority has a broad possibility. You can overstep your authority if you kill somebody from a firearm without the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. necessary circumstances. So I used that form and term assuming that that was the case. Of course, when we speak about killings we mean with intent, premeditated. Here there was no intent, I'm quite sure, of killing anybody. I don't know the specific circumstances that surrounded the event, but from this we can see that a criminal report was filed and the court acted upon it. Of course, the description as to the policemen's behaviour and conduct is in a way not very clear and was probably written on the basis of just one source of information. Your policemen here are very cordial towards me, although I'm a witness, if I can put it that way and use the example. And of course I could add that this description is a description on the basis of facts presented by one side. I believe that in the police files and the case there are other facts as well, and I do believe that this description does not include all the information and facts compiled by the police unit where the event took place. Of course, I don't know and cannot say whether that is absolutely true, but I do believe it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, let me put the thing to you generally. Please listen. And we may look at one more report, either just before or just after the break, if the Court's disposed to take a break. In the course of 1993, three different organisations recorded against your police excessive brutality, physical and mental, shooting people dead, killing people in police stations, displacing Albanians from their homes, using excessive violence against demonstrators, mishandling and arresting journalists. That can be found in the range of reports that are available to us and, if the Court wishes to see them, available to the Court. First of all, is it your case that the authorities will have carefully considered all of those serious, grave allegations made by independent bodies?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my case that careful consideration was given to all concrete, specific events described in the allegations. Now, if a policeman or a group of policemen in one specific case applied excessive force the consequence of which resulted even in death, it doesn't mean that the police in Serbia was violent and that the police in Serbia instilled fear. So let me repeat: Very often one can conclude that one or two or three events which cannot of course be justified, nor is it anybody's intention to justify them, tend to be generalised and conclusions drawn from it on the functioning of the police as a system. That is something I cannot accept. And even the defence described - I accept that they happened if you tell me - and in the latest one we can see that the police did not, as you say, hurry to -- that it did what every police force is required to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you -- and again it's your evidence that I'm testing. Can you identify any other Western society which to your knowledge has received this level of recurring complaint about brutality by the police in the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point in time, of course I cannot because I don't have information about something like that. But bear in mind, please, the kind of security situation and security related problems Serbia was confronted with at that time. You cannot compare the security situation and security threats in Serbia during that period of time with the situation, for example, in Holland or in some other West European country. They were very specific and complex circumstances in which the police force had to deal in quite an extraordinary way, faced with the security problems. It had to protect the borders, it had to prevent the war from spreading into its territory, it had to contend and fight terrorism as the core and source of all problems. It wasn't the police that caused violence in Kosovo. The police fought against violence. And you have to fight violence, among other things, by using force sometimes. If you cannot --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Another interpretation which I'm going to suggest to you both in respect of the reaction of the police to peaceful demonstrations already seen and in the reaction of the police under your command to demonstrations at the end of 1996 and 1997, when the accused was slowly giving way to recognising democratic votes in local elections, we'll look at that later, but I'm going to suggest to you that the violence of the police was aimed at retaining power for this accused and you know it.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you mentioned 1996 and 1997. I assert, and you can check this out in all the video archives, that three months -- for three months the police was very peace loving and tolerant, and for three months the police activities out in the open from those three months, you can extract just two or three sequences where you can see police violence. But let me repeat, they are typical exceptions, because you're not showing us everything else that goes to the advantage of the Serb police force and what it was doing for three months, three months of maximum tolerance without a single instance of violence. And then in one day there was intervention, and you know full well how difficult it is to forecast any intervention once it is unleashed when there is violence, and then from that you film ten or 15 seconds of violence and you make your conclusions about the violence that -- violence of a whole police force. That is quite unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're going to take the break now, Mr. Nice. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to move to a new topic almost immediately, Mr. Stevanovic, but before I do, just this: You will accept, will you not, that at least the three bodies I referred to before the break continued reporting on police brutality, violence, killings, and expulsion of Kosovo Albanians right throughout the period 1993 to 1998?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot agree with that because I don't have the relevant facts in my possession. But again you ask me a question, "You will agree, will you not," or "You will accept, will you not." If I say "No," will that mean that I accept or I don't accept? If you cannot change the way in which you formulate your questions, of course I will have to adjust, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, you perfectly well understand what I'm driving at. Do you accept or do you not accept that there was reporting on the police alleging extreme brutality of a criminal kind right throughout the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It sounds easier now. There were reports in that sense, but they cannot be qualified in the way you qualify them, that the police was brutal and so on and so forth. There were events in which the police overstepped their authority or applied force contrary to the law and in which certain consequences occurred, as we have already discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, amongst the exhibits that touch on this, which I haven't the time nor the present disposition to go into, are 188, 190, 204, 205, 772, and 773.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: These are reports by whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They're a range of reports from either Mazowiecki or Human Rights Watch. They cover various aspects of life in the former Yugoslavia, but all of them include passages on police brutality and similar and they cover a wide range of topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are in addition, Mr. Stevanovic, as you know, reports published by the Humanitarian Law Centre, and I want to ask two questions about that, or three of you. You said earlier today that those reports are biased. Does that mean that you've read them in order to say they're biased?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some parts of those reports I have read. Certainly a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All I want to know is do you accept that those reports wherever possible name victims and give details of circumstances so that you, the authorities, could, if you chose, investigate further?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those reports or, rather, parts of reports that I've read cite certain incidents, and those that contain factual information were, I repeat, subject of police attention and verification. The reason I said they were lopsided and biased is that those reports predominantly speak of violence against Albanians and say nothing or next to nothing against -- about violence against the innocent by terrorists. Almost nothing is said about the murders -- I would like to finish. Next to nothing can be read about murders, mutilations, intimidation and terror against uninvolved and innocent citizens, leaving aside policemen and soldiers. That is the reason why I call this reporting biased and one-sided. Maybe there are other reports --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This witness makes long answers to every question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, he was explaining why he characterised the reports as biased, and I think he's entitled to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The question was whether these reports named victims and details so that further investigation would have been possible. My third of three questions, Mr. Stevanovic, which is appropriate in light of your last answer, is this: Are you aware that Natasa Kandic, who is the principal of this humanitarian organisation, humanitarian rights organisation, has indeed published material about the suffering of the Serbs? Just yes or no will do. Are you aware that she's done that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I want to move on now. In a sense moving on. You told us that you went to Kula in 1996 and are aware that there was a similar -- another anniversary in 1997. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the first part of your question I can answer yes. To the second part also yes. I found out about that other anniversary in 1997 from an interview in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: An interview had by whom with whom?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With your investigators. Approximately three months ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to have played a portion of the video of the 1997 anniversary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's, of course, already an exhibit. We have made available for you some -- I think they really count as courtesy copies of the transcripts that you've already got as an exhibit, because otherwise it would be difficult to follow or more difficult to follow something when the screen is occupied with the -- yes. Just -- I'll revert to the previous point while the matter is literally in my mind and the book is in my hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Natasa Kandic, Mr. Stevanovic, was publishing a book on the disappearance of non-Albanians in Kosovo. I take it it's not a book you've ever acquainted yourself with, that you've ever read? This is an English version, but --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but it's possible that I have read some of it. I'm not sure, I repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the point you make -- or made, Mr. Nice, was that she was publishing about violence towards Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Non-Albanians is inclusive of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It could be, but are you telling us it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Serbs and Romas I think are the two categories that are specifically dealt with. Can we now play this. There are certain segments, and Your Honours will see in the courtesy copy provided the segments are outlined in black line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Nice. What is the year of the publication of that book?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll find out and get back to you. If the publication date isn't given, the context will identify it probably. The transcript was already exhibited as 390. There have been one or two, I think, corrections made on this version for sense, and I don't know whether they're on the 390 original. Can we play the first clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We should be getting a translation over the headphones. I'm sorry we're not. It would help if we could have one.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have a copy of this transcript that they can find.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let a copy of the transcript be passed to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I gather one has been passed to them. Mostly this is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. largely ceremonial at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Members for the unit of special operations, greetings. "Greetings."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That will do, thank you very much. The rest is words and not ceremonial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You recognise there, do you not, the man Legia? Milorad Lukovic.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The man - and this reverts back to what I said right at the beginning - the man now charged with the assassination of Djindjic.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Allegedly under an operation code named Stop The Hague.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the commentary in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next clip, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Mr. President, veterans of the Special Operations Unit of the Republic of Serbia state security are lined up for inspection. Colonel Zika Ivanovic reporting. "Hello, Colonel Ivanovic. "Mr. President, allow me to introduce the unit's veteran officers. Mr. President, Colonel Radojica Bozovic. "Milosevic: Hello, Bozovic. I read those reports of yours. "Colonel Bozovic: Thank you. God forbid there should be more of them ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Help me with this, Mr. Stevanovic: This colonel, it appears, has written reports that have been read by the accused. What would be the content of reports written by somebody ascribed the rank of colonel? Would they be operational?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends on the subject of the report or the orders received. Based just on this question, I cannot give you an answer. I don't have sufficient facts. I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been in the army. What rank -- what military rank did you hold as a reserve officer when you were promoted to general in 1995?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already answered. In 1990 but not later than 1993, I held the highest rank in the police force at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before that --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rank that I had while I was assistant minister is not the highest possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, please listen to the question. What was the highest military rank you ever held? Because you finished military academy.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I graduated from the military academy and was then given the rank of second lieutenant in the army. Later on I was promoted in the reserve force of the army and I held the highest rank of captain, or maybe major. I wasn't particularly interested because my profession was policework.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In -- I dare say. But a colonel reporting on the activities of his troops is going to be providing, is he not, a review of what has been accomplished by him and his troops. Yes?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, every leader in general submits reports of that kind to his superiors. The act of writing a report does not say much about the contents. It is the rank that tells us more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We should have to know what assignments this colonel had, what his --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Colonel Dusan Borovic. "Milosevic: Pleased to meet you. "Colonel: Likewise, Comrade President. "Colonel Ivanovic: Colonel Vasilje Mijovic. "Milosevic: Pleased to meet you. "Colonel Ivanovic: Colonel Goran Opacic. "Milosevic: Hello. "Colonel Ivanovic: Colonel Predrag Prica. "Milosevic: Pleased to meet you. "Colonel Ivanovic: Lieutenant Colonel Zvezdan Jovanovic. "Milosevic: --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We don't seem to have a picture of Zvezdan Jovanovic, but that's a name known to you as well, isn't it, Mr. Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, since he was charged with murder. I know about him since he was arrested and charged with the murder of Prime Minister Djindjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll move to the next part, the next clip, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Mr. President, we thank you for accepting the invitation to attend the ceremony marking the anniversary of the formation of the Special Operations Unit of the State Security Service. It was constituted on the 4th of May, 1991 at the time of break-up of the former Yugoslavia, and since it emerged it has constantly worked to protect national security in circumstances where the existence of the Serbian people was directly jeopardised throughout its entire ethnic area. Its combat operations were anti-terrorist, directed at preventing war crimes, mass retaliation and genocide. "From the first moment of its existence ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No reason to doubt what Frenki Simatovic is saying about this unit, whatever it was called, being constituted on the 4th of May of 1991?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made a similar statement in my interview some two months ago in Belgrade because that question was leading, in a way, and I didn't want to go into greater detail and deal with the question more deeply because I was in the capacity of a suspect, and I wanted to focus on issues that had to do with my own work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No question at any time of Frenki Simatovic's unit being subordinated to the army?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether the unit of Frenki Simatovic was resubordinated to the army, to the best of my knowledge it never was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I never asked myself that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From all the material available to you and to us, his unit was either subordinated to the MUP or personally to the accused. Which was it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This unit that we are discussing here now was part of the sector of state security; therefore, part of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But more precisely within the sector of state security.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Due to the international circumstances we are all well aware of, we were forced to operate in complete secrecy. And despite wartime conditions: Fighting with Croatian and Muslim troops, the presence of numerous United Nations international forces - later IFOR and SFOR - and numerous instruments of foreign intelligence services in the field where the unit is not --" the rest is inaudible. "The contribution of the Special Operations Unit is enormous. Forty-seven soldiers were killed and 250 wounded in combat operations at 50 different locations. We are proud of the unit's level of professional training, which meets the highest international standards, and the unit has never experienced defeat. One of its most recent successes was its engagement in the freeing of 400 UNPROFOR hostages in Republika Srpska, which met with a very positive response in the international community and made our country's position stronger. One of the unit's most successful actions in our territory was the capturing of the National Guard Corps terrorist group, caught in the Apatin area in 1993. "Mr. President, allow us to inform you briefly about the unit's history, its combat record, present situation and function. When it was formed, its corps was made up of members of our service, Republic of Serbian Krajina Police, and volunteers from Serbia. The Second War Service Intelligence Administration, which was also set up at the time, included a special team for offensive and logistical support of the Special Operations Unit. "From the 12th of October, 1991, in battles with armed Croatian police forces --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just from the passage we've just been listening to, a secret organisation; correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I understood him as saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Including --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Including people identified as volunteers from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Press on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] ... in the zones of Benkovac, Stari Gospic, Plitvice, Glina, Kostajnica and others, the unit provided important support in the liberation of all areas of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Around 5.000 soldiers were engaged in these battles and their actions were coordinated by the unit Command and an intelligence team from the Second Administration. "In May 1991 an air-helicopter squadron was formed which transported tons of special shipments, equipment, troops and machinery from the improvised airfields of Medeno Polje, Petrovac, Velika Popina, Srb, and Udbina and carried out numerous complex tasks while war operations were ongoing. "In September 1991 a part of the unit was transferred to Serbia, where its reconstruction was conducted and high-quality professional training organised."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Incidentally, the man standing beside Milosevic, or the accused, is of course Stanisic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
