utterances.text: That is Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far on this part of the tape the places described as places where the unit went with Croatian police forces in Benkovac, Stari Gospic, Plitvice, Glina, and so on, those are not places about which you told us when you gave evidence a couple of days ago, are they?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are not the places.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that because you weren't kept informed of where these units were fighting or because you chose not to mention these places?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's absolutely not the case that I decided not to say something that I know. Whatever I know I will say loud and clear. However, what I heard now from this footage in no way corresponds to what I know. That's one. And second, everything I heard here is different than the words of the same man in another speech in 1996. I know that the description Frenki Simatovic gave in 1996 of the activity of his units was much different from this one, and he described the traditions of his own units in a drastically different way than what we hear here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you have -- sorry. Do you know if there is a video recording of that ceremony?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether there is a video recording. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move on with the video, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] These two units were involved in operations in Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Twenty-six training camps for special police units of Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina were also formed in that period. In the Republic of Serbian Krajina in Golubic, Dinara, Obrovac, Gracac, Plitvice, Samarice, Petrova Gora, Licki Osik, Benkovac, Lezimir, Ilok and Vukovar, and in the RSK, Republic of Serbian Krajina, in Banja Luka, Doboj, Samac, Brcko, Bijeljina, Trebinje, Visegrad, Ozren and Mrkonjic Grad. "Units of Serbian [inaudible] joint operations in Eastern Slavonia, the corridor of Brcko, in the Drina, Sarajevo, and Maglaj operations. In Western Bosnia, the unit was the backbone of Fikret Abdic's army with around 15.000 soldiers who freed most of the Cazin Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, the training camps identified and the places this unit served, vastly different from the places you identified in the territories of Croatia and Bosnia a couple of days ago. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned only those places where certain assignments were executed by special police units, and I named specifically the places that I visited. The presence of units from Serbia in these places quoted here is something I know nothing about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If that's true, and if what Frenki is saying is accurate, does that mean that the DB of the MUP was kept hermetically sealed from the state security?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the MUP there is both the sector of public security and the sector of state security. In organisational terms, state security was clearly divided from public security, but of course both these sectors belonged to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And ultimately answered to this accused.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They answered to the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To whom did he answer?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He answered to the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So is it --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had certain responsibilities toward the president of the republic, as I've already explained, which was to submit a report to him on his request. However, the minister was a member of the cabinet, and he was responsible to the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On your understanding of the accused's structure of government, can you explain how that colonel's reports were read by this accused?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't believe he did read these colonel's reports. I believe he read the minister's reports, in accordance with the law. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why do you believe that? You heard the words he said. Why should they be interpreted differently from how they read?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear him say that he had submitted a report to the president. Perhaps I overlooked it. I am basing my previous replies on my general knowledge. I did not deal with the links between the minister and the cabinet or the minister and the president. It's simply something I know about from my general knowledge. I did not attend either cabinet meetings or meetings in the president's office apart from those few meetings I did attend which I have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to what you say are the differences between the 1996 and the 1997 accounts given by Simatovic - one that you heard of, one on the tape - are you asking us to consider that Simatovic was making up this account to this accused?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe -- well, it's hard to reach this conclusion, and I've been thinking about why he did that, and the only thing I can conclude is that he wanted to portray himself in a favourable light before the president of the republic, and this is usually a part of such reports on such ceremonies when somebody wants to advertise his unit and its tradition, to promote it. I believe that in that previous year, with respect to the activities of members of his unit, he ascribed to them things done by other units. It might be a good idea to look at a video, if there is one, of the ceremony in 1996, because then we could see whether I'm right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you're -- incidentally, have you had an opportunity to discuss this with Mr. Simatovic after he was interviewed by the investigators? Have you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you not see this video on national television when it was broadcast in 2003?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was able to see part of this video from this trial. I didn't see this part. I did see the review, but I didn't really follow it in great detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So your proposition includes that Simatovic would make up details about the establishment of training camps and about fighting battles in territories of Bosnia and Croatia when he did no such thing. That's really what you're asking us to believe, is it, as possible?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not insisting on anything you're supposed to believe. I'm just telling you what I know, but my reply here was really about what I think, what my opinion is, because that's how your question was formulated, if this deserves special attention to be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So here we see Stanisic pointing out on a map to the accused. Pause there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember to whom that plaque was dedicated?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not, no. And you can't see anything on this video clip. I don't remember any similar plaque.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember that the centre now bears the name, or did at a recent stage, Radoslav Kostic?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it did bear the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He died in action in 1994. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember when he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pausing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you went there in 1996, did you see that map?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see a map. I don't know whether it was this map and whether this is what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, it's marked with places, as we can see and hear, where it is said actions took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we lay on an overhead projector first of all one version of that map overdrawn with the markings for Bosnia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does this look to you to be the map that you saw in 1996? It's a relief map. It's not a flat map, it's in relief.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I saw this map. In fact, I'm sure I didn't see a map like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Have a look at another -- that's from the video. Now have a look at another version, please. Same map, same overmarkings, but there have been some town names put in, or some location names. Showing, in Bosnia, Bosanski Samac, Brcko, Bijeljina, Doboj, Zvornik; all places referred to the video and all places for which we have evidence of action having taken place during the course of this war. You told us before -- or you told us in answer to a question of the accused this: "I am aware of all the engagements of the police of Serbia outside the territory of Serbia."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I still abide by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you told us about a few events happening on the east of Croatia and Vukovar and thereabouts and a few activities on the far east of Bosnia. Do you have any reason to doubt that this unit of Simatovic operated on all those places and others, but all those places marked on the map and now named?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two questions in my mind. First of all, all the geographical terms I mentioned I abide by, but the names mentioned here that I did not mention are something I know nothing about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Next clip, please.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, special purpose police units were also in Western Bosnia, not just Eastern Bosnia, as you said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Mr. President, dear guests, let us pay tribute to Deputy Minister Radovan Stojicic Badza by observing a minute of silence."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pause there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Badza was your boss and he was assassinated, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in a minute we're going to look at another event concerning that. We'll just end with this video first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next clip. Next clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The video ends with -- we can see Legija on the left, the accused, and Stanisic on the accused's right, now on the accused's left, reviewing the military equipment. I'm not going to take time doing that, but we'll just get to the first vehicle and then perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you went there in 1996, did you see a personnel carrier, an armoured personnel carrier that had been seized from the Dutch at Srebrenica there?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw more than one vehicle, but I don't know that a vehicle was taken from the Dutch in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's deal now very briefly with Badza Stojicic's, or Badza as he's known, funeral. Gunned down as he was, he had a benefit of a large ceremony.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pause there. We can see middle, dead centre, Arkan. To the left of the screen in the darkened glasses, Sainovic; to Badza's right -- sorry, to Arkan's right we can see Lilic; to his right, obscured by a hat, we can see the accused. Press on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now the next, please. And now this:

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] For Radovan Stojicic there were no secrets in policework. He participated directly in numerous very complex actions in which he showed exceptional courage and commitment. Radovan Stojicic did not demonstrate his patriotism by talking about it but immediately on the scene of events taking part in them, always wherever this was most necessary and most difficult."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So this is, on your account, the leader of the police, the national state police. What patriotism was required of somebody running just the national state police?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's logical that patriotism is required of everybody. Everybody living in a country should love his country and be prepared to defend it. That's what I understood by that word.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what were the complex arrangements that he was dealing with? Were those events across the border in Croatia and Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already explained the complexity of the situation in Serbia in the 1990s and compared those conditions with those in other countries. This is not easy to compare. I am aware that Mr. Stojicic spent time in Baranja and Eastern Slavonia during 1991 or 1992 when I was in Kosovo and Metohija, but he was not there with his units, but according to my information, he went there as an individual. Perhaps some other members of the ministry were there with him, but as far as I know, certainly there were no units of the Ministry of the Interior there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And is the truth this: That Badza's patriotism which you praised, for it was you speaking at that funeral, was the same quality looked for in the JSO?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And that was Serb patriotism. I'm going to deal with the former Yugoslavia. It was the interests of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Verbally, criminals can also be classed as terrorists who call themselves patriots. The word "patriot" is a positive word, but it can take on different meanings, depending on who uses it and in what way. The way I used here was in a positive sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And finally, how could Badza with his senior position before he was killed, have gone as an individual to these other territories? How could he have done that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that at that time I was in Kosovo dealing exclusively with the tasks presented to me by the situation and the leadership. I really do not know specifically according to what model he was there. What I do know is that he was not there with units. I know that he was appointed a leader there, whether of the Territorial Defence or something similar I don't know, but he was not leading a unit. According to what model he spent time there, whether as a volunteer or in the form of some sort of cooperation, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was it these complex events of which you were ignorant that you referred to elliptically in your funeral address when you spoke of the complex missions he'd been engaged on?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course this was a long time ago. My opinion is that when I referred to complex events, I was not referring to any events outside Serbia. Serbia was confronted with enormous problems. The police of Serbia was facing enormous challenges. Of course this doesn't apply just to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anyway, you know how eulogies are written and what they're Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. supposed to contain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you be good enough, please, with Mr. Prendergast's assistance, to look at the original of this document, the English copy of which can be placed on the overhead projector, it being Exhibit 277. Is this a document you've seen before?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the first one, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let's read it together then. Oh, no, sorry, it's not that document. That's the covering letter. The next document, please, Mr. Prendergast, in English, and the accused, I hope, has the second document, dated 1997. Is this a document you've seen before?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document, the covering letter is something I have certainly not seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're concerned with the fundamental -- the underlying document. Have you seen that before?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just read it. I don't think I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What it reads, and we'll read it together: "During the period of preparation for passing the law on carrying out the security affairs of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the Department of the State Security will perform its duties in accordance with the guidelines of the President of the Republic and the Republic of Serbia government ..." Signed by this accused, dated April 1997. Completely unconstitutional, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not a question for me, whether it's constitutional or not. I really don't know, because it does refer to an article of the constitution. I have not seen this document before. I have heard something about this, but I really don't know what the purpose of this document was or why it was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... tell us what you'd heard about it.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I heard about this from a broadcast emanating from this Tribunal, but I can't say I understood it very well. As for the document, I repeat, I've never seen it before, and I don't know when and under what circumstances it was compiled. This is the first time I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You remember when I asked you a question a little earlier about the lines of the DB reporting to this accused. You corrected me straight away and said no, not at all, it goes up to the government. Can you explain how in 1997 it would be necessary for this accused to have the DB formally answering to him in the way this document suggests?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know that. I would have to look at the document more closely. I didn't even understand it as saying this, that the department of state security was answering to the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: To be more precise, it says that "The Department of State Security will perform its duties in accordance with guidelines of the President of the Republic ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and the government of the Republic of Serbia. What this means in effect I really can't say at present. What I know now is that the department of the state security was subordinate to the minister of interior affairs. This is the first time I've seen this document and I don't know what it means. I have the impression that you're putting questions to me that fall outside my sphere of competence, but of course that's your right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In 1997, according to witnesses in this Tribunal, Bakalli and Haxhiu, the following people, Gajic, Stijovic, and Hadzic, gave details of a Serb policy that then existed in respect of Kosovo. Now, Gajic was what, Stanisic's deputy?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to David Gajic who was in Pristina? I don't know. It's possible he was an assistant. He was certainly one of the high-ranking leaders in the sector for state security, and in Kosovo I think he was the leader of some kind of coordination centre of the state security department, but I'm not sure of its precise title.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Since the decision purports to be pursuant to Article 83 of the constitution of the republic, it would be useful to ascertain what that provision says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll add it to my list of things to do. There's something that was outstanding from the first session that I've not delivered on, and indeed I've forgotten what it was. I'm sorry about that. There was another document you wanted me to bring and I've forgotten it. It'll be on the transcript and we'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, on the evidence we've had, in late 1997 Gajic and others spoke of the Serb authorities having a plan described as burnt or scorched earth. "Sprzena zemilja," I think. Were you aware of a plan with such a title?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was never such a plan. I have no knowledge of that plan. I am certain that in the police, in the Ministry of the Interior, no such plan existed. And I'm also certain it did not exist at the level of the state, because this would run totally counter to the government policy and the policy of the Ministry of the Interior. It would be contrary to all the facts that I am aware of. Of course one would have to know what is meant by that concept, but I assert that such a plan with such a title or such a code name is something I have never seen in my life and I assert that such a plan never existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just moving ahead for a second before we return to the chronology. Generals Clark and Naumann met with this accused in the autumn of 1988 for the October agreements. Were you there?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I've already said, for three days and two nights I was at the negotiations with that NATO team.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you there then on the occasion which shocked those witnesses, they explain, when the accused said that why didn't he do what had happened in 1945 at Drenica, kill them all? Were you there when he said that to Clark and Naumann?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did attend several meetings there but I absolutely do not remember that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go back, then, to June. You're aware, aren't you, that a decision was made that there should be direct authority through assistant ministers for the administration of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Minic and others, including Sainovic, came to be running a body called the Joint Command, didn't they, in 1998?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have explained everything I know about the joint command. It's correct that in the sense in which I explained it Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Minic were members of that body, as well as Mr. Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The idea for that body, do you accept, as we've heard, came from this accused at first -- or not necessarily first but certainly once being adumbrated by him at a political party session of the SPS in June of 1998?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not follow political sessions. Quite possibly there was an idea like that. Now, whose it was specifically I don't know. What I do know is what was in the field and how it functioned in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, that, incidentally, is D142A, I think as an exhibit. Defence Exhibit 142. You remember I asked you right at the beginning of questioning whether the position throughout the 1990s was that the accused ran anything of significance, military eventually and also police, and for Kosovo do you accept that a decision as to how to administer Kosovo in 1998 would inevitably have needed the approval of or been made by this accused?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I can't say. I don't know that. I know exactly how the Ministry of the Interior functioned in Kosovo, of course, and I also know that the staffs of the ministry in Kosovo and Metohija functioned from 1990, perhaps 1989. The staffs the federal ministry from 1981. Therefore, what I can say with full responsibility and fairly exactly, that as far as the Ministry of the Interior goes, the organisation and structure there of the police organisational units practically remained unchanged from the 1990s right up until 1999. All that changed were the personnel, the composition of the staff in Pristina and the leaders of individual organisational units. However, the system remained intact, unchanged, throughout all those years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next can we consider in a short summary what was being said of Kosovo by Human Rights Watch in 1998? This is Exhibit 191, so we'll place page 4 in the English -- 4, top left-hand corner, Mr. Prendergast -- on the overhead projector. And, Mr. Stevanovic, I'm going to read out a summary from Human Rights Watch, an organisation you have not yet criticised for lack of objectivity, and it says as follows: "The first major government offensive began in mid-May, a few days after Milosevic agreed to US demands that he meet with Rugova. The special police, together with the Yugoslav army, attacked a string of towns and villages along the Albanian border -- along the border with Albania in the west, with the specific intent of depopulating the region. Until then, the UCK had been receiving arms and fresh recruits from across the border." Do you accept that summary of events for the early part, perhaps the spring of 1998?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That resume is -- or summary is absolutely incorrect for the spring of 1998. And for the spring of 1998, to the best of my recollections, I can say that the sole activity which the police undertook in the territory of Metohija was linked to the deblocking of the Pec-Djakovica road or communication line. And the only and basic aim of that operation was that. So nothing about depopulating anyone or any attacks on any settlements of any kind. No retaliation regarding the Albanians, just to deblock the roads and to ensure safety and security in the passage of citizens between the two towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What about the single sentence: "Until then the UCK had been receiving arms and fresh recruits from across the border"? Would that appear to be fair and accurate?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to arms, that is quite certain. As to the recruits, I'm not quite sure at this point in time. Probably that is true too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll read you the next paragraph. "Many villages from Pec in the north to Djakovica in the south were shelled while civilians were still present. Non-combatants who fled the attacks were sometimes fired on by snipers, and a still undetermined number of people were taken into detention." Accurate or inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Settlements weren't shelled in the sense that we explained shelling. So the use of police weapons were aimed at eliminating people from opening fire on the police and aimed at deblocking the road. I think that a relatively small number of people were arrested, and I'm quite sure that snipers -- that there was no sniper fire against civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The report goes on to suggest that in three cases helicopters marked with Red Cross emblem reportedly fired on civilians. Was there, to your knowledge, abuse of the Red Cross emblem?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am certain that there was not. The Red Cross emblem was worn by military helicopters. I used such a helicopter once or twice for transporting injured or wounded policemen towards Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the last part --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I never saw any weapons in a helicopter of that kind. And as I said, I used the services of that helicopter at least two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then to conclude this paragraph, it reads as follows: "Landmines were placed in strategic points along the border as well as along the southern border with Macedonia. Most villages in the region were looted and systematically destroyed, and farmers' livestock was shot to ensure that no one could return in the short-run. 15.000 people fled to Albania and an estimated 30.000 went north to Montenegro." Now, is there any part of those sentences that you accept as an accurate account?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the last quotation seems to be a semi-truth. There was indeed quite a lot of livestock that had suffered, and there was partial moving and internal displacement of persons. However, the basic context of this quotation is not accurate. That was not the objective --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who shot the livestock? You're not going to suggest -- yes?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the livestock was certainly not shot intentionally, killed intentionally. In the combat zone is where the livestock were. You have meadows between villages and settlements in the area and zone under the control of the terrorists. Of course, not too many livestock were killed. Not a lot of cattle were killed, but I just said that I know that some of the cattle was killed because I moved along those areas. And that is what you usually see when there's a war. You could see that throughout Kosovo, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally for this report, it interprets government activity, towards the bottom of the page, as an apparent attempt to crush civilian support for the rebels, and in the last paragraph on the page says that the majority of those killed and injured had been civilians and that there were about 20 -- at least 250.000 people currently displaced, many of them women and children living with their families or without shelter in mountains and woods. Do you accept that there were a large number of civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that there was displacement, persons displaced, but this figure is certainly not accurate, and certainly there were civilian casualties. However, this number and the extent to which these are mentioned here, the problem is mentioned here, has not been realistically assessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the goal -- that goal did absolutely not exist, and I think that in the quotation you read out there was mention of a goal and objective. I told you what the goal and objective was. That's quite clear. Of course the police nor any other state organ did anything against civilians intentionally as a goal, especially not to prevent them from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What would your assessment be of the civilian casualties and persons displaced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we're talking about this particular period, the figure is exaggerated because those villages quite certainly along the roads don't have that number of inhabitants, a total of that number of inhabitants. So there could have been several thousand displaced, a maximum of several thousand. Not tens of thousands. Here we have hundreds of thousands mentioned. That is absolutely unrealistic. You couldn't reach that number anyway, even if you were to count all the displaced persons: Today, 10.000; tomorrow 10.000. Perhaps if you added them up in that kind of way you might reach that figure, but over a longer period of time that figure -- or, rather, in that period of time the figure could not have been anywhere near the figure mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where did you get your figures from? Did the Serb side keep a record of displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that that was my assessment. During that period, I don't know whether any records were kept. And it was very difficult to keep records anyway because you had to rely on assessments and estimations, and I said that this was my particular assessment, although when you read out the text I understood you to say that several hundred thousand people had been displaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 250.000 was the estimate of Human Right Watch.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the dozen or so villages this is an unnaturally large figure. Compare it to the number of Albanians in Kosovo, the population, and you will see that this is not realistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You became intimately involved in the events in Kosovo from about this time onwards, didn't you, as a member of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a member of the Joint Command, but at that time I did spend quite a significant number of days in Kosovo. Nobody ever told me that I belonged to any command at all, including the Joint Command. I did -- I was present on several occasions at meetings for people who said -- whom we said could come under the name of members of a Joint Command, but only in the sense that I explained it. I think that was during the first couple of days of my testimony here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Joint Command was meeting sort of every day, every other day, wasn't it? It was a hands-on body.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My information tells me that those people did meet very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Headed by either Minic or Sainovic and reporting directly to whom? The accused?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me say I don't know who was at the head of it. The structure was such that who was first and who was second was never established, and to whom they reported I really don't know. When I was there, I reported to the minister. General Lukic, I assume, and I'm almost certain that he reported to the minister too. Now, who Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Minic reported to I really don't know, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've got a lot of reports of activities from various MUPs, I imagine. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in a position to use the reports of the organisational units of the Ministry of the Interior. Not always, but always when I was in a position to avail myself of those reports. When I was in Kosovo, for example, I wasn't able to use the reports of the other secretariats outside Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you get to know, for example, about units, groups of people who were doing bad things? Let me remind you, for example, of one; the group called Munja. Do you remember about Munja?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember different names of the Osa, the Wasps and the Munja and so on, different names. The names of insects, birds, and so on were used. Now, I can't link that name up with a specific group at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it's time for the break. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have Article 83 for you, if I can hand that in. It's part of Exhibit 319, tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, so that we can proceed in an orderly way, by 1998, residents of Kosovo were subject to the influence or effect or force of the rising KLA. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The residents of Kosovo and Metohija were under the influence and pressure of the KLA, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the other hand, they were facing a Serb government absolutely determined in its objectives.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but in its objectives against terrorism, not against the citizens of its own country.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Serb government was now effectively represented by delegated powers run through the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kosovo, there was a provisional provincial Executive Council, and as I understand it, that was the body that represented state authority in Kosovo and Metohija. Perhaps I'm not quite right in saying that, but that's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, we don't -- do we want that on the overhead projector at the moment? No. Thank you, Mr. Prendergast, that's just for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Pass it to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pass it to the Judges. I'm sorry. I didn't see that was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're not really suggesting, are you, that the provisional Executive Council exercised real power over the MUP or the VJ or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The provisional Executive Council didn't have authority over the army or MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, Andjelkovic appeared at or was a member of the Joint Command and the provisional Executive Council thus responded to the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody reported to the Joint Command. They made up people from different structures but at the same level. And the Joint Command and its work boiled down to, as I have already said, an exchange of information, horizontal cooperation, and so on, of different state organs, including the police and the army and the Executive Council of Kosovo and Metohija, and representatives of other state organs from Belgrade as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Going back to my earlier question that the Serb government was absolutely determined in its objectives, the citizen of Kosovo, if he wasn't facing pressure or force even, or violence by the KLA, was facing effectively a determined police state.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The citizens of Kosovo and Metohija were not facing a police state. I have been repeating this several times now. The terrorists were facing the effects of a state combatting terrorism, but the citizens were in that surroundings, and of course that overall situation had to have an effect on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If a citizen of Kosovo was confronted by a Serb policeman, that Serb policeman would be almost the absolute power that he had to deal with, wouldn't he? There would be nobody else to whom he could turn.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The citizen of Kosovo in principle was not confronted with the police. The police was on the side of the citizens, against terrorism and crime and all other forms of threatening law and order in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If a policeman stopped somebody on the street and said, "Come to the police station with me," for no known reason, the citizen would have little choice but to comply.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the same relationship on the whole territory of the republic as it was in Kosovo. The police, in conformity with its authorisations, does have the right to call a citizen to come to the police station once conditions for that are met. So there's nothing different there in Kosovo and Metohija. No different conduct towards the population of Kosovo and Metohija than was practised in other parts of the Republic of Serbia. Perhaps I haven't understood your question properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Was the level of violence that the citizen in Kosovo could be -- could expect to find in the average police station enormously greater than that which he could expect to find in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean violence, unlawful use of force, then excessive behaviour on the part of the police force in Kosovo and other parts of the republic could be equated except for the fact that when there was a clash with terrorists in Kosovo and Metohija there were more cases and incidents where the citizens suffered as well, which was not the case in Serbia. But in principle, excessive violence by police towards citizens was equally possible inside Kosovo and outside Kosovo. The same applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Look at this document, please. It's Exhibit 320, tab 9. My suggestion to you is that not only was Kosovo now by the middle of 1998 a dangerous and frightening police state for these confronting the services of the police, but the structure was further dangerous because the police were acting together with illegal groups, paramilitaries of one kind or another. This, you see -- I hope you've got the original version there, Mr. Stevanovic. This is a document --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- from the Republic of Serbia MUP dated the 24th of June and coming from Pec, and it says: "Report on the measures and actions taken to protect damaged and abandoned property and on the legality of police actions during the Operation Thunder ..." And it says this: "During the aforementioned period, the three platoons of the 3rd Company of the 24th Detachment of the special police unit ..." I'm pausing there. The special police unit is the public MUP. It's your organisation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "... were directly subordinated to --"

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Public security, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: " ... were directly subordinated to the JSO. "While we were carrying out this operation, platoon Commander Vidomir Salipur was hurt." Now, Salipur was one of the Munja paramilitary groupings. You can see that in many places. It's well evidenced. What was your police group doing working with someone like Vidomir Salipur?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all - I have just refreshed my memory - I think that that name Munja, as you said, belonged to a police detachment from Pec, and this man Mr. Salipur was in that composition. He was a member of the active police force. Therefore, I'm quite certain that he didn't belong to any paramilitary group at all, and at that time different police and even military units called themselves in some way, gave themselves a name. Usually it was like a code sign from the communications centre. So if the call-sign was Jastreb or Sokol, a bird name, for example, over a longer period of time that name came to be associated with it and it took on this name, the name it took on from the code name in communications and signals. So I assume that this name Munja referred to that department Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which was from the Pec special units composition to which Mr. Salipur himself belonged. But I can say with certainty that we're not dealing with any group outside the composition of the police and the PJP. It's not even a reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pause, please, just to have a look at this picture and caption from "Under Orders", Exhibit number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be given a copy of the document that was provided to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Let a copy be provided. That should be done as a matter of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I haven't yet received the document they were told to hand over to me at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you put this on the overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, the document is coming the accused's way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Including the one that you were told to hand over.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. We will find that and make that available to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, this is one account of the man Munja. I will read you the caption in English. "Witnesses identified the man on the right as --" no, further out, I need to read the caption, sorry. "-- as Nebojsa Minic, known as 'Mrtvi' or ('death'). He is implicated in the extortion and killing of six family members in Pec on June 12. On the left is Vidomir Salipur, a Pec policeman and alleged head of the Munja gang ..." Does "Munja gang" sound about right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, stop. I'm not satisfied with the attitude towards this matter of handing over the documents to the accused. Has this particular document been handed over to the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. If Mr. Prendergast would make the one that's been placed on the overhead projector available to the accused, that can happen. For the one for this morning, we'll get another copy provided for that as soon as we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Bear in mind that he may -- it may be something that he needs for his re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, Munja gang; was Salipur the head of a gang?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Prosecutor. That name, that term "gang" is derogatory. We're talking about a unit from the composition of the special units of the police. We're talking about an active policeman or leader, I'm not quite sure which, but an organisational unit of that kind, of the police, cannot be termed gang in any way. A gang is group of persons committing crimes on -- along the lines of organised crime. And as to the other name, I have no knowledge about that. Possibly he was a member of the police, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, just to alert you, the published material that includes this particular exhibit we've been looking at has Munja as the leader of a group that on the 12th of June in 1999 killed six members of one family including children aged 5, 6, 7, 12, and 13. Do you know if that's a crime you ever investigated?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of that crime. Of course if the crime took place, it is a crime, and I never questioned that nor do I do so now. Now, whether the quotation is proof of that or whether it is just information from one source, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we have, please, the minutes -- or the notes, rather, of the meetings of the Joint Command. Do we have copies of those for the accused as well as for -- right. So we have here for the overhead projector and for the accused meetings of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija in the original language for you, Mr. Stevanovic, and in English for the overhead projector. That will suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I'd like you, please, just to turn to a few entries. First, the 29th of July in the original, please, Mr. Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Prendergast, if you look at the bottom right-hand page, you'll see a number of 164. Could you take us to page 24 of 164. Beg your pardon, 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, do you have the entries there, Mr. Stevanovic, for the 29th of July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I cannot find it very quickly. If somebody can help me, it would be a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you can't find --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have 30, and the one before that is probably 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you'll see an entry by General Pavkovic towards the beginning of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And he is recorded as saying: "There is still a region between the villages of Crnolje and Dulje to be cleaned." I want to ask you two questions on this page and you might as well have the context. A couple of lines further down, he says, "The goal from phase 1 has been fulfilled and we can be satisfied." Are you able now to remember what the three phases were of which this was phase 1?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember perhaps an earlier date. I know of the existence of three or perhaps four phases in the combat against terrorism. They were operationalised in the unified plan for combatting terrorism which I mentioned in my earlier testimony, but I am not sure at this moment whether this particular passage is a reference to that. I don't see what it could --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Okay. My second question is --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- be reference to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- what is meant by "clean"?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in principle, I've answered that question as well. This term "clean-up" means cleaning the territory from terrorists. There is another meaning and that is clean-up in terms of sanitisation, as remarked by one of the Judges some time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- summary of activity in May described by Human Rights Watch. This is a couple of months later. Are you sure "cleaned" doesn't have a rather more sinister meaning and it means clearing people out?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By no means. By no means can that term "clean-up" be linked with the clearing of territory of people or citizens. It can only mean clearing of a territory from terrorists. That is the only meaning that can be attached to this concept. Of course, you can use any concept and place it in a negative context, but that would require a certain bias if that intention is to be fulfilled.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could you move, please, to the 12th of August in the original. Can you move to the 12th of August and go to the first entry of Mr. Sainovic, which is early on in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Prendergast, it's page 50 of 164, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, this, take it from me, if you'd be so good, Mr. Stevanovic, is a meeting at which you were present because indeed we see you referred to on page 51 of the English. Don't worry about that. But where you're looking at now -- further down the page, please, Mr. Prendergast, yes. It's the second entry by Mr. Sainovic, we see him saying this: "In the border belt, the army is to look at its obligations. "In this area, the police are to cover all the --" we don't know what the word is -- "territory and consolidate. "DB -" the secret police or security - "are to cover and take over the third area." Doesn't this note show clearly that the Joint Command was a command and that it was under civilian authority?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my view, that's not what it shows. We can only talk about the ways certain things are expressed or the way notes are taken. This could have been just an opinion of Mr. Sainovic, but by no means could it have been an order for the police to act. For the police to act, it would have had to receive orders from General Lukic and Lukic would have had to receive orders from the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are we going to find --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. Are we going to find in these notes anywhere resistance by Lukic to instructions effectively given him one way or another by Sainovic or Minic? Is that your recollection? You were there at many of these meetings. Or are we always going to find that what Minic and Sainovic said went?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really cannot answer this question easily. I would need to analyze the whole material in order to do that. But what is important is to see whether what Mr. Sainovic said needed to be done was indeed done the next day and who issued the orders. From this material, I cannot see that, I cannot make that kind of analysis. But I do know that for any serious assignment of the police regarding terrorism the orders had to be given either by the staff or the secretariat or the minister himself through the staff and the secretariat. So the orders of Mr. Sainovic or Minic could not have been executed --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have authority to give orders as an assistant minister?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have powers to issue orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page, please, Mr. Prendergast.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it's, for you, the first entry by yourself. Yes, there we are. We see you saying, "The 3rd and 4th did not participate and really should become engaged." Then Minic breaks in, and Minic, at numbers 8 and 9 -- right at the bottom of the page, please, Mr. Prendergast -- says: "Refugees and civilians are eager--" something illegible -- "on us such a humanitarian catastrophe, but we have to call on them to return to their homes, and that is where the main strikes will take place." Can you recall what all that meant?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I don't remember that sentence and I don't know even now what it could possibly mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What could main strikes on them in their own homes mean?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It does not say main strikes on them in their own homes, as Mr. Nice is trying to represent. It is very hard to read, but there is a reference to refugees and civilians, indeed. It says that they should be convinced to return home. That is incompatible with strikes on their homes. Maybe Mr. Stevanovic is better able to read this handwriting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot find the line.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Para 8, item 8: "Refugees and civilians ..." It's on the next page. "We need to appeal to them to return to their homes."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He can deal with it perhaps in re-examination when they've had a chance to look at it more carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. You may take this up in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 26th of August, next, please, Mr. Stevanovic. I have only got another two of these to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are, of course, documents which will take a great deal of time to go into exhaustively. They are available for general review. I can only take us to a few points. Page 74, Mr. Prendergast.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And for you Mr. Stevanovic, probably the second page, where Mr. Radovic speaks. Radovic is speaking. I don't know if you found this place in the original, and he says: "There are 16 to --"

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it's very difficult to make out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the interpreters have made out the following for the contribution of Mr. Radovic under his sixth bullet point: "There are 16 - 17.000 of people that took refuge in Albania, and 40.000 people that took refuge in Montenegro." Then it goes on about one journalist Batun says Klaus Kinkel is losing in his theory that the autonomy will probably fail and then something about the solution being unacceptable for Milosevic, but I'm just interested in these figures of refugees because it comes from these people attending this meeting. Can you remember discussion about refugees on this scale?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent some time to find this quotation, and I didn't follow you very well. You say it's on the first page, 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first entry line, Mr. Radovic, which is probably the first -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the second -- the second entry by Mr. Radovic, actually. And it's probably on the second page or thereabouts, and it's got bullet points. 16 to 17.000 people took refuge in Albania, 40.000 in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the month of August, if that is when it is written. I really have no reason to doubt it at this moment, but I'm really unable to find the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From what were these refugees fleeing?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the 26th of August, from what I recollect, was a period when several anti-terrorist actions took place, mainly in the area of Metohija, and it's very possible that this is related to those anti-terrorist operations. But I repeat, I cannot place this accurately in time. I proceed from the assumption that this is what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you go over to the next page of notes, I think it will be, where your name first appears. And it's page 75 for Mr. Prendergast. Can you find your first entry on this note, or the first entry of what you said.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The same date.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it possible that my pages are all mixed up? I really cannot find my own name anywhere. And we are talking about the 26th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, 26th of August, 8.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radovic, Gajic, again Radovic, then Sainovic. Ah, here. Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say there is a big movement of civilians near somewhere or other, we don't have the full name. "If we continue, we will have a general movement of civilians." And then if you look down three entries to somebody's contribution who can't be identified but the contribution stands, and somebody says this: "Return of civilians with recognition of Serbia without weapons and there will be the police to keep order." Do you find that entry?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Don't take any more time. Can you give any explanation -- it's at the bottom of the page. And in the original it is very hard, of course, to read. The interpretation -- the translation is only that which is legible to the translators. You can give no explanation for this period of 1998 why there should be so many thousand people on the reckoning of those present at this meeting taking refuge in Albania or in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me again those numbers? 16 to 17.000 in Albania, 40.000 in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my belief that that was a period of major anti-terrorist operations in the area of Metohija and it is possible that these figures are related to the operation that I told you about when I was explaining the return of several thousand people to their villages from a place called Istinic. That's what it could be but I cannot place it accurately in time. Also, it is very realistic that there was a movement of citizenry at the time. I don't remember this particular meeting, although it is obvious that I attended it, so I cannot give you any additional comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My next question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Explain how an anti-terrorist operation would cause people to flee.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I tried to explain more than once the reasons for such movements of citizenry. In places where the police clash with terrorists, the citizens move, and I explained why. Out of fear and out of their own desire to find cover while the anti-terrorist operation is going on, but also because the terrorists themselves tried to get civilians to move to create a semblance of humanitarian catastrophe, sometimes using them as a shield. There was sometimes pressure by international organisations to have those civilians return. For whatever reason, this movement happened. We on our part wanted people to return to their homes as soon as possible, and we took every step to achieve that, but such movements did occur, among others in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... huge population movements is that under cover of what might have been legitimate anti-KLA action, Serb forces, police, and VJ operated the scorched earth policy that had been mentioned earlier to people like Mr. Bakalli?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is an absolute fabrication. It has nothing to do with the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may rest assured of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... two things. Shall we go to the 27th of August. My last entry, I think certainly at this time, on these documents, which will be page -- the first page of it. This is the 27th of August. You see? The very first entry by General Lukic. Top of the page. We see -- that's fine. Perfect. We see at the end of the first block of type, and I hope you can find in the original -- by the way, there was a note taker at these meetings, wasn't there, Mr. Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is obvious if this is an original copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it says: "The route Suva Reka-Orahovac is open without any major -" something or other. Now, that's what's recorded in the note of the meeting. I'd like you to attend, please, Mr. Stevanovic, to the evidence we have heard from Lord Ashdown, of whom you will know, who gave evidence about what he saw on the 27th of August, pages 2354 and onwards. He said he came round a corner to see Suva Reka, the whole of the valley which forms a sort of amphitheatre for this area. By the way, do you remember, Mr. Stevanovic, the geographical shape of the Suva Reka area? Does Lord Ashdown's --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- description of it as lying in a form of amphitheatre fit with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could describe it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you can visualise as I read on what Lord Ashdown says he saw. He says he was deeply shocked by what he saw, as was the British ambassador, who had been informed by the Yugoslav government that operations which were continuing against the Drenica villages of Kosovo had stopped the day or two days before, because what he saw was an entire amphitheatre of hills in which every village was ablaze, and they both saw and heard reports of shell-fire, and they saw the explosions. Can you explain from the notes we've seen and your assertion of how the forces conducted themselves, can you explain how, if Lord Ashdown is believed as accurate, he saw this?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the description, although it seems specific, is nevertheless rather general. In that area, to the best of my recollection, there were indeed clashes with terrorists at the time. I will repeat once again: I am certain there was no shelling of villages. That wording does not apply to all I know about these operations. It is possible that the anti-terrorist operation in question covered a large area including what you call this amphitheatre since it is positioned geographically in that particular way and in view of the fact that it is desirable to conduct an anti-terrorist operation at the same time in all the components of one area. It is possible that traces of fire were visible in that region at the time. Fire is something that normally accompanies anti-terrorist operations sometimes, but you cannot say that the whole amphitheatre was ablaze or that shelling was common practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You may not know, but Lord Ashdown has his own military experience, was in company with another military man as well as the ambassador, and he told the Court that in their judgement, artillery was being fired from the Dolje Blace feature that runs - I don't know if it's north/south, east/west there - at some 7 to 10 kilometres from the villages concerned. And he went on to explain that they could hear and see the strike of shells, they could hear the boom of artillery. Their judgement was that it was T-54 tanks probably and certainly tank fire, that it was certainly 120-millimetre artillery, possibly as large as 150. And he went on to say that there was the strike of mortar with its particularly characteristic sound, and their estimate was of 82-millimetre and perhaps 120-millimetre mortars. That's the evidence. Is that what was being done to the villages of Kosovo under cover of dealing with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing was done under any pretext. What was done I explained more than once. I do not challenge the fact that in certain anti-terrorist operations artillery was used, including mortars. Sometimes recoilless guns, too, sometimes even tanks. I personally did not observe the use of tanks myself. However, all the weaponry that you named as being used was used, I'm absolutely sure of this, to achieve a legitimate goal, that is not to shell villages but to neutralise terrorists and their leaders. The artillery fire that we are discussing was mainly used in absolutely open areas, clearings, and against fortified terrorists positions. Whether there were any exceptions to this rule, whether a specific feature was targeted that was a gun emplacement of the terrorists or another fortification, I don't know. I can only tell you about things I have personal knowledge about, and this is not the case here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Incidentally, as to the police weaponry, did I understand you to say that the police had anti-aircraft guns?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did have anti-aircraft machine-guns, usually mounted on APCs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And were these used, in the course of dealing with the KLA, for firing at houses?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that these were used only in order to neutralise groups of terrorists if they were inside such buildings; houses or other buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By "neutralise" you mean eliminate, don't you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not mean to eliminate in the sense of killing but in the sense of repelling a unlawful attack. The term "elimination," too, has a broader as well as a narrow sense and it means more than just killing. To eliminate terrorism also means eliminating terrorism by making terrorists disarm and disband their organisation. That is one of having them eliminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did it occur to you as perhaps excessive force to be using an anti-aircraft machine-gun against a house that contains individuals?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Against the house containing citizens, yes. But against the house from which fire is opened at the police, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could just trouble you then for one further reference in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Prendergast, page 128 in the English, I think. And it's the 25th of September. If you would be good enough to find that in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you found the 25th of September?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I'm close to it. Just a minute. Yes. It's just one page, if I -- if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think if you -- I think if you turn over from the first page you'll come to the first contribution -- I beg your pardon, the second contribution from General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if Mr. Prendergast could take us to page 129 on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General, have you got the entry by General Pavkovic for this date, the 25th of September, which begins: "The operation in the area of Donje Obrinje and Gornje Obrinje is finished. Resistance was strong, but this group was squeezed into a smaller area. "The lack of participation of the JSO resulted with the following consequences..." and so on and so forth. But -- perhaps I should read the next sentence: "After the death of one police officer from the MUP police force, the operations were temporarily stopped. Actions from the south contributed in completion." It does say, "Continue clearing tomorrow," you can see that further down, and it suggests enemy losses, about 200 people. First of all, do you remember this incident yourself personally or not?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know which incident is referred to, but after the 21st of September in my text, I see the 25th. That's only one paragraph on one page, so I have the impression we are not looking at the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're quite right. It's the 26th. My error. If you go to the 26th, you'll see the passages I've referred to under General Pavkovic's name.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you think that 200 deaths at Suva Reka, recorded as having happened by the 26th of September, show proportionate or disproportionate force?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could respond to this if I knew what area was covered by the anti-terrorist actions and for how long they lasted. From what you have read out, if I followed well, this does not refer to Suva Reka at all because Donje Obrinje, if I recall correctly, is in Glogovac municipality. This is on the other side of a large watershed in relation to the area you mentioned before, the amphitheatre, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Move to another area now. We're now concerned with Obrinje, the two Obrinjes. Does it seem to you that within the area of Obrinje these 200 losses is disproportionate use of force?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this number is highly suspect to me. I don't believe this information is correct. I would be surprised if General Pavkovic mentioned that number. This is probably just an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Roughly what would be the population in that area, of that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would depend on the area covered. But if we're referring only to those two villages, then it might be seven, eight, or 10.000 at the most. I am completely sure that such a small area was not an area that would be covered by an anti-terrorist action.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, the reason I choose this as an example for you to deal with is that we've had evidence from a Mr. Abrahams, the man who works for Human Rights Watch and prepares some of their reports, and he visited Donje and Gornje Obrinje on the 29th of September, a couple of days later, with a man called Bouckaert, and when they arrived bodies were being taken out for burial, one of them an 18-month-old child. In the woods there were seven bodies, including of five women and two children, who had died from head wounds. They spoke to local residents and although it is clear there was fighting in that area, it was also clear that the members of the Delijaj family had been murdered, civilians who had been taking refuge in the forest. Now, we see a total of 200 casualties as ascribed to the enemy, and we have on the ground an investigation that suggest innocent and young civilians have been murdered. Does it look to you as though there may indeed have been disproportionate use of force?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The killing of those five or six civilians - I am not sure how many exactly were found - is indisputably a crime. This must not be linked with the members of terrorist groups who were possibly killed. But I did not see anything here that would confirm the figure of 200 killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you see, they also went and visited Gornje Obrinje -- sorry, from Gornje Obrinje they went to Glogovac, where they heard of 13 men being executed in a yard, lined up and executed. Executions of that kind could never be justified, could they?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not. But as you yourself said, they only heard about it, so this information was not verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Maybe it fits, you see, with the very large number of casualties of which General Pavkovic, on the record, was content to speak.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, this is most probably an estimate, and you yourself counted ten at the most based on this document, and this is hugely disproportionate to the estimate you mentioned. Only civilians are listed, and that is indisputably a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to break from my current exploration of documents, to which I must, I am afraid, return to tomorrow, but ahead of tomorrow's questions I want a little general assistance from you. First in relation to Racak. The accused has asked you a lot of questions and brought you here to produce a lot of documents. What is the position? Are you able to help us with what happened at Racak or not?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the facts I know I have already mentioned in response to questions by the Prosecution. Perhaps you can assist me by putting additional questions to me and I will certainly tell you everything I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the map, first, shall we? Or in fact it's not a map, it's an aerial view. Are you capable of reading aerial views, with your experience in the police and earlier in the army? Are you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps you'd take one of these maps and see if there's one there that the general would like to look at in order to, with his pointer, tell us what happened at Racak, because that's what I'd like to know from you. If the aerial doesn't help, tell me, and we'll approach it in another way. But if the aerial does help, then a picture being worth more than a thousand words, you can lay it on the overhead projector and with the pointer tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
